lead: Every receiver picks up unwanted random voltage along with the signal. Electrons jostle in resistors, charges cross junctions at random, and the antenna collects whatever the city radiates. We cannot predict this noise sample by sample; we can only describe its statistics. Modelling it as additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) — flat in frequency, Gaussian in amplitude, added to the signal — reduces the whole physical mess to one number, the noise power inside the receiver bandwidth. Every signal-to-noise ratio and error-probability result in this subject starts from that model.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for the Gaussian PDF and 1.5 for power spectral density and autocorrelation.

blocks.text: Every resistor generates a random voltage because its electrons are in constant thermal motion. This is thermal noise, also called Johnson noise. It needs no current to flow and cannot be designed away — only cooling the resistor or narrowing the bandwidth reduces it. It sets the noise floor of every receiver, from an FM radio in a Chennai flat to a satellite earth station.

blocks.where: P is the available thermal noise power in watts; k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant; T is the absolute temperature in kelvin; B is the bandwidth in hertz; R is the resistance in ohms; vn is the RMS noise voltage in volts. Power does not depend on R, but voltage does: a larger R delivers the same available power at a higher voltage.

items: Shot noise: charges cross a junction at random instants. i² = 2qIB, where q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge, I is the average DC current in amperes and B is the bandwidth in hertz. It appears in diodes, bipolar transistors and photodiodes.
Flicker noise: surface traps capture and release carriers, giving a PSD that rises as 1/f. It dominates below a few kilohertz; the frequency where it meets thermal noise is the flicker corner.
Burst noise: a defect switches current between two levels at random, heard as popping in a speaker. It is a faulty device, not a law of physics.
External interference: lightning, motor ignition, nearby transmitters. These enter through the antenna and are fought with shielding and filtering.

blocks.text: White noise is the ideal noise whose PSD is the same at every frequency, as white light holds every colour. Its two-sided PSD is S(f) = N0/2 W/Hz for all f. N0 is the one-sided PSD in W/Hz, the density you get when only positive frequencies are drawn. For a resistor at temperature T, N0 = kT.

blocks.where: S(f) is the two-sided PSD in W/Hz; N0 is the one-sided PSD in W/Hz, equal to kT for thermal noise; R(τ) is the autocorrelation of the noise; δ(τ) is the Dirac delta, infinite at τ = 0 and zero elsewhere.

blocks.text: The autocorrelation is a delta. Any two samples of white noise, however close in time, are uncorrelated. A delta is infinitely tall and infinitely narrow, so the total power is infinite. White noise is a model, valid only over the band the receiver actually uses.

Power in a bandwidth. Noise that passes through a filter with positive-frequency width B carries power P = N0B. The same formula holds for a low-pass filter and for a band-pass filter far up at 100 MHz — only the width matters, not the position.

Equivalent noise bandwidth. Real filters have sloping skirts. A single-pole RC low-pass with 3 dB bandwidth B_3dB collects noise over the whole tail; its equivalent noise bandwidth is B_n = (π/2)B_3dB ≈ 1.571 B_3dB. Put B_n, not B_3dB, into N0B or kTB.

sections.h3: Gaussian noise, the AWGN channel and SNR

blocks.text: Thermal noise is the sum of an enormous number of independent electron motions. The central limit theorem makes that sum Gaussian, with zero mean and variance σ² equal to the average noise power.

blocks.where: p(v) is the probability density of the instantaneous noise voltage v in volts; σ² is the average noise power (in watts across 1 Ω); σ is the RMS noise voltage in volts.

blocks.text: White plus Gaussian gives AWGN. The model makes three commitments: the noise adds to the signal, its amplitude is Gaussian, and its PSD is flat. The received waveform is r(t) = s(t) + n(t), with s(t) the wanted signal and n(t) the noise. This additive white Gaussian noise channel is the most used channel model in the subject; every error-probability formula in Unit 5 and Unit 7 assumes it. It fits a thermal-noise-limited receiver. It does not fit impulsive interference, and it does not fit fading, which multiplies the signal instead of adding to it (see Unit 6, Digital Passband Modulation).

SNR. Signal-to-noise ratio is average signal power divided by average noise power in the same bandwidth: SNR = P_s/(N0B), where P_s is the signal power in watts. In dB, SNR(dB) = 10 log10(P_s/P_n). A receiver with 1 mW of signal and 4×10⁻¹⁵ W of noise has SNR = 2.5×10¹¹, that is 114 dB. Digital work usually quotes Eb/N0, energy per bit over N0, which is independent of bandwidth (Unit 5 and Unit 7).

figure.caption: The signal and a white Gaussian noise source meet at a summing junction; the receiver sees their sum and passes only the noise inside its bandwidth B = 1 MHz. Notice that the noise spectrum is flat, so bandwidth alone decides how much noise power gets through.

spec.title: AWGN channel model
spec.aria: A signal source and a flat-spectrum AWGN source feed a summing junction whose output goes to a receiver of bandwidth 1 MHz.

examples.question: A 1 kΩ resistor at T = 290 K feeds a receiver whose equivalent noise bandwidth is 1 MHz. Take k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K. (a) Find the available thermal noise power in watts and in dBm. (b) Find the RMS noise voltage. (c) Find the one-sided noise PSD N0 in W/Hz and dBm/Hz.
steps: Given: R = 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω, T = 290 K, B = 1 MHz = 1×10⁶ Hz, k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K.
Available noise power: P = kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1×10⁶ = 4.002×10⁻¹⁵ W.
One-sided PSD: N0 = kT = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 = 4.002×10⁻²¹ W/Hz, that is −174.0 dBm/Hz. Check: N0B = 4.002×10⁻²¹ × 1×10⁶ = 4.002×10⁻¹⁵ W, which matches step 2.
examples.answer: The available thermal noise power is 4.00×10⁻¹⁵ W (−114.0 dBm), the RMS noise voltage is 4.0 µV, and N0 = 4.002×10⁻²¹ W/Hz (−174.0 dBm/Hz).
examples.check:
import math
k = 1.38e-23
T = 290.0
B = 1.0e6
R = 1000.0
P = k*T*B
dBm = 10*math.log10(P/1e-3)
vn = math.sqrt(4*k*T*R*B)
N0 = k*T
N0dBm = 10*math.log10(N0/1e-3)
print(f"{P:.3e}")
print(f"{dBm:.1f}")
print(f"{vn:.3e}")
print(f"{N0:.3e}")
print(f"{N0dBm:.1f}")

traps: White noise has infinite total power. A statement like 'the noise power of this resistor is 4 fW' is meaningless until a bandwidth is fixed; look for the B or N0 the question forgot to give.
N0 and N0/2 differ by 3 dB. Integrating the two-sided PSD from −∞ to ∞ uses N0/2; integrating the one-sided PSD from 0 to ∞ uses N0. Mixing them makes the answer wrong by a factor of 2.
Noise power P = kTB does not contain R, but noise voltage vn = √(4kTRB) does. Doubling R doubles vn² and leaves P unchanged — examiners test exactly this.
dBm and dBW differ by 30 dB. 4×10⁻¹⁵ W is −114 dBm but −144 dBW. dBm is referenced to 1 mW, not 1 W.

'White' and 'Gaussian' describe different things: white is the shape of the PSD, Gaussian is the amplitude distribution. Noise can be white and non-Gaussian (impulsive), or Gaussian and band-limited (not white).

quiz.q: Define white noise and write its two-sided PSD and its autocorrelation.
quiz.a: White noise has a constant PSD at all frequencies: S(f) = N0/2 W/Hz for every f. Its autocorrelation is R(τ) = (N0/2)δ(τ), a delta at τ = 0, so samples at different times are uncorrelated.

quiz.q: State the Johnson–Nyquist formula for available thermal noise power and define each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: P = kTB, with P in watts, k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K, T in kelvin and B in hertz. Drawn as a source with the resistance, vn² = 4kTRB with vn in volts.

quiz.q: Why is thermal noise described by a Gaussian PDF?
quiz.a: It is the sum of a very large number of independent random electron motions. The central limit theorem makes that sum Gaussian, with zero mean and variance equal to the average noise power.

quiz.q: A datasheet states that a resistor produces 4 fW of noise. Why is the statement incomplete?
quiz.a: White noise has infinite total power, so any finite figure must come from a finite bandwidth. The 4 fW is the power after a filter of some width B, because P = kTB; without B, or without N0, the number means nothing.

quiz.q: A receiver has one-sided noise PSD N0 = 4×10⁻²¹ W/Hz and bandwidth 200 kHz. Find the noise power in watts and in dBm.
An RC low-pass filter with 3 dB bandwidth 10 kHz sees white noise of N0 = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Find the noise power at its output.
quiz.a: Equivalent noise bandwidth B_n = (π/2)B_3dB = 1.571 × 10⁴ = 1.571×10⁴ Hz. Output noise power P = N0B_n = 4.0×10⁻²¹ × 1.571×10⁴ = 6.28×10⁻¹⁷ W.

quiz.q: In a lab, doubling the receiver bandwidth doubles the measured noise power, but doubling the source resistance leaves the available noise power unchanged. Explain both observations.
quiz.a: P = kTB is linear in B, so doubling B doubles P. The same formula has no R in it: a larger resistance develops a larger noise voltage (vn² = 4kTRB) but must be matched to a larger load, so the available power stays kTB.

beyond: Not for the exam. A real receiver adds most of its noise in the first amplifier, not in the antenna, which is why the low-noise amplifier sits immediately after the antenna and why the next chapter's noise figure matters more than raw gain. At microwave and optical frequencies the classical kTB floor fails and the quantum term hf must be added. In CMOS design, 1/f noise sets the floor of baseband analog blocks and is fought with chopping and larger devices. Software-defined radios move filtering into software, but the noise bandwidth of the ADC obeys the same rules. Search next for noise spectral density, equivalent noise bandwidth, ADC noise floor and phase noise.
